title: CAN YOU LOVE JESUS AND SECRETLY LOVE LUST?
paragraphs: CAN YOU LOVE JESUS AND SECRETLY LOVE LUST?

The question is not whether temptation ever enters your mind. The terrifying question is what happens when you invite it to stay—and whether the secret thing you keep feeding is slowly becoming the thing you refuse to surrender to Christ.
There is a version of you that everybody sees.
The version that smiles.
The version that says, “God is good.”
The version that shares the Bible verse.
The version that worships when the song reaches the chorus.
The version that knows when to say “Amen.”
And then there is the version of you that nobody sees.
The version alone with a phone.
The version behind a locked door.
The version scrolling when everyone else is asleep.
The version that knows exactly what to search.
Exactly what account to visit.
Exactly what memory to replay.
Exactly which conversation has crossed a line.
Exactly which fantasy you keep returning to even though something inside you whispers…
You know this is not where Jesus is leading you.
Maybe nobody knows.
Your spouse may not know.
Your parents may not know.
Your pastor may not know.
Your friends may not know.
The people sitting beside you at church may never imagine the war happening behind your eyes.
But Jesus knows.
And before shame convinces you to stop reading, you need to know something else.
Jesus knowing is not the end of your hope.
It may be the beginning of your freedom.
Because the Christ who exposes darkness is also the Christ who walked toward scandalous people when everyone else stepped away.
So stay with me.
Especially if part of you already wants to leave.
Because perhaps the most dangerous question is not, “Have I ever struggled with lust?”
The more penetrating question is:
Have I begun protecting what Jesus is asking me to surrender?
There is a difference.
A massive one.
Temptation can knock on the door without your permission.
A thought can flash through your mind.
Your body can react.
An image can appear.
An attraction can happen.
You can feel temptation intensely and still choose obedience.
Jesus Himself was tempted, yet Scripture says He remained without sin.
Hebrews 4:15 says that Christ was “tempted in every way as we are, yet without sin.”
So temptation itself is not proof that you do not love Jesus.
Please understand that.
A believer may genuinely love Christ and still experience fierce sexual temptation.
A believer may stumble.
A believer may have wounds, habits, memories, and patterns that require serious discipleship and patient sanctification.
A believer may fall and come crawling back to the throne of grace.
The Christian life is not the story of people who never face temptation.
It is the story of sinners who increasingly learn where to run when temptation comes.
But there is another condition entirely.
It is possible not merely to be tempted by lust…
but to feed it.
Schedule it.
Protect it.
Romanticize it.
Return to it.
Hide it.
Make excuses for it.
And eventually become angry whenever Jesus puts His finger on it.
That is where this question becomes uncomfortable:
Can you love Jesus while secretly loving lust?
Listen to Jesus Himself.
In Matthew 5:28, the Greek reads in part:
“πᾶς ὁ βλέπων γυναῖκα πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι αὐτὴν…”
pas ho blepōn gynaika pros to epithymēsai autēn…
In context, Jesus teaches that whoever looks at a woman with the purpose of lusting after her has already committed adultery with her in his heart.

The important word is related to the Greek verb ἐπιθυμέω — epithymeō, meaning to desire or long for. The word itself can describe desire in different contexts, but here the construction and context make the sinful direction unmistakable: Jesus is confronting a look cultivated for lustful desire.
Jesus takes the issue deeper than external behavior.
He goes into the heart.
That means you can keep your hands technically “clean” while allowing your imagination to become a private bedroom for sin.
You can never physically touch the person.
Never meet them.
Never sleep with them.
Never get caught.
And still nurture something inside that does not belong to Christ.
That is frightening.
But it is also strangely hopeful.
Because Jesus is not merely interested in making your browser history cleaner.
He wants your heart back.
Pornography promises intimacy without covenant.
Lust promises pleasure without responsibility.
Fantasy promises possession without relationship.
Secret sexual sin whispers that you can take what you want from another human being in your imagination without having to love that person as someone made in the image of God.
And it always asks for another look.
Another video.
Another fantasy.
Another conversation.
Another compromise.
Just one more.
Until “one more” becomes tonight.
Then tomorrow.
Then next week.
Then years.
And eventually you are not simply watching something.
Something is discipling you.
That screen is teaching your eyes what to hunger for.
Your repetition is teaching your brain what to anticipate.
Your secrecy is teaching your conscience when to become quiet.
Your fantasy is teaching your heart to consume instead of covenantally love.
And meanwhile, Jesus stands at the center of Christianity saying something radically different.
Not:
“Manage your lust better.”
Not:
“Hide it more successfully.”
Not:
“Become respectable enough that nobody discovers it.”
Jesus calls you to Himself.
This is why Paul writes in 1 Thessalonians 4:3:
Touto gar estin thelēma tou Theou, ho hagiasmos hymōn…
“For this is the will of God, your sanctification…”
And Paul immediately connects that sanctification with abstaining from sexual immorality.
The Greek word ἁγιασμός — hagiasmos carries the idea of holiness or sanctification—being set apart to God.
Notice what Christianity offers.
Not merely restriction.
Consecration.
Your body is not garbage.
Sexuality is not dirty.
Marriage is not dirty.
God created human beings male and female.
God created covenant.
God created marital union.
The Bible does not oppose sexuality because sexuality is too powerful.

Scripture guards sexuality because sexuality is powerful enough to wound, bind, unite, betray, create life, communicate covenant, and touch places in the human heart that casual consumption can devastate.
Lust takes something sacred and asks:
“How can this satisfy me?”
Love asks:
“How can I honor God and seek the true good of this person?”
Lust consumes.
Love gives.
Lust reduces a person to what their body can make you feel.
Love remembers there is a soul inside that body.
A soul God sees.
A soul Christ calls to repentance and redemption.
A soul that was never created to become raw material for your fantasy.
And perhaps that hurts to read because you know exactly where this reaches into your life.
Maybe it is pornography.
Maybe it is not.
Maybe it is the coworker you keep imagining.
The married person you keep messaging.
The ex whose photographs you still visit.
The account you unfollow and then search for again.
The “innocent” flirting you would never want your spouse to read.
The private folder.
The deleted history.
The second account.
The saved videos.
The explicit fiction.
The emotional affair you refuse to call an affair because nobody has touched anybody.
Maybe it is not even something another human being would easily discover.
But God already has.
Psalm 139 declares that there is nowhere we can flee from His presence.
That should terrify hypocrisy.
But it should comfort the repentant.
Because the God who sees you completely is the God you no longer need to hide from.
Adam sinned and hid.
Human beings have been hiding ever since.
We hide behind bushes.
Behind religion.
Behind ministry.
Behind marriage.
Behind humor.
Behind theological vocabulary.
Behind deleted histories.
Behind “everybody struggles.”
Behind “at least I never actually did anything.”
But grace does not grow in pretending.
First John 1:9 tells believers that if we confess our sins, God is faithful and just to forgive us and cleanse us from all unrighteousness.
The Greek word translated “confess” is ὁμολογέω — homologeō.
At its heart is the idea of acknowledging, admitting, saying what is true.
No more renaming darkness so you can keep it.
No more calling bondage “just how I am.”
No more calling deliberate fantasy “just attraction.”
No more calling secrecy “privacy” when privacy has become the hiding place of rebellion.
Call it what God calls it.
Then bring it to the God who already knows.
Because repentance is not merely feeling disgusting afterward.
Repentance is not crying tonight and arranging another encounter with the same sin tomorrow.
Repentance is a turning.
It is agreeing with God strongly enough that your direction begins to change.
Sometimes dramatically.
Sometimes painfully.
Sometimes with trembling hands deleting what you once protected.
Sometimes with installing accountability systems.
Sometimes with handing another mature believer access to the places where secrecy has been feeding you.
Sometimes with confessing to a trusted, mature Christian who will refuse both to crush you and to flatter your sin.
Sometimes with ending the relationship.
Blocking the account.
Removing the app.
Changing the routine.
Moving the device out of the bedroom.
Refusing to negotiate with yourself at 1:00 in the morning.

Jesus uses shocking language in Matthew 5 when He speaks of tearing out an eye or cutting off a hand if it causes sin. Christians have historically understood this as deliberate hyperbole, not a command for bodily mutilation. Jesus is communicating the radical seriousness with which sin must be treated.
In other words:
Stop petting what is killing you.
You cannot crucify something while simultaneously making sure it remains comfortable.
And this is where someone will ask:
“But if I keep failing, does that mean I never loved Jesus?”
Not necessarily.
Peter loved Jesus and failed catastrophically.
He denied even knowing Him.
Three times.
At the moment when loyalty mattered most.
And after the resurrection, Jesus went looking for Peter.
Not to pretend Peter's denial did not matter.
Not to tell Peter that betrayal was harmless.
Jesus restored him.
Grace did not call Peter's sin acceptable.
Grace made Peter's failure something other than the final chapter.
That is the Gospel.
The Gospel is not that good people learned to control themselves.
The Gospel is that sinners could not save themselves, so the Son of God came for them.
Jesus lived the righteousness we have failed to live.
He went to the cross.
He bore sin.
He died.
He was buried.
He rose again.
And forgiveness is offered not because you finally became sexually flawless enough to deserve Jesus…
but because Jesus is sufficient to save sinners who come to Him in repentance and faith.
That distinction changes everything.
You do not clean yourself so Jesus will finally love you.
You come to Jesus because your attempts to save yourself have failed.
Then the grace that forgives you begins teaching you to say no to the things that once mastered you.
Titus 2:11–12 says that the grace of God trains us to renounce ungodliness and worldly passions and to live self-controlled, upright, godly lives.
Did you catch that?
Grace trains.
Real grace does not merely pardon.
Grace transforms.
Not instant perfection.
Not sinless performance.
But a new allegiance.
A new war.
A new direction.
A new hatred for what separates your heart from obedience.
A new hunger for Christ even when the old appetites scream.
This is why the real warning is not that a Christian experiences temptation.
The warning is when you stop fighting because you have secretly decided the sin deserves a permanent room in your heart.
There is a difference between falling in battle and signing a peace treaty with the enemy.
One says:
“Jesus, I hate that I keep falling. Help me.”
The other eventually says:
“Jesus, You may have everything except this.”
And Christianity gives us no safe category for intentionally crowning Christ as Lord while permanently reserving one protected kingdom where He is forbidden to rule.
Jesus said in John 14:15:
“If you love me, you will keep my commandments.”
That does not mean obedience purchases His love.
It means love for Christ bears fruit.
Imperfectly.
Sometimes slowly.
Sometimes through tears.
Sometimes through repeated battles.
But genuinely.
First John 2:15 says, “Do not love the world or the things in the world. If anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him.”
Scripture does not permit us to make peace with cherished rebellion and then use the language of grace to make ourselves comfortable.
Yet Scripture also does not permit us to tell the struggling believer that every temptation proves he or she is abandoned by God.
Conviction says:
“Come into the light.”
Condemnation whispers:
“Stay hidden because God could never want you now.”
The Gospel says:
Come.
Not because the sin is small.
Because the Savior is greater.
Come while ashamed.
Come while shaking.
Come after the relapse.
Come after the failure you swore would never happen again.
Come honestly.
But come ready to surrender.
Romans 8:1 says:
“There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.”
And Romans 8 does not stop with freedom from condemnation. It speaks of life in the Spirit and putting to death the deeds of the body.
Grace and holiness are not enemies.
The same Jesus who refuses to condemn those who belong to Him refuses to leave them enslaved.
Maybe you have prayed:
“Jesus, forgive me.”
And then failed again.
So you prayed again.
Then failed.
Again.
Again.
Again.
And now you wonder whether your prayers mean anything.
Do not measure the power of Christ by the number of times temptation has knocked you down.
Look instead at what you do when you become conscious of your sin.
Are you running from Christ?
Or running toward Him?
Are you defending the sin?
Or confessing it?
Are you arranging opportunities to fall?
Or beginning to destroy those opportunities?
Are you merely terrified of consequences?
Or increasingly grieved because your sin dishonors the One you love?
Do you want Jesus merely to remove your guilt?
Or do you actually want Him to become Lord over your desires?
Be honest.
This may have hit harder than you expected.
Maybe your hands are holding a phone containing something you know needs to disappear.
Maybe somebody's name immediately came into your mind.
Maybe there is a conversation you already know must end.
Maybe your secret has survived because nobody has ever forced you to say it out loud.
You do not need to tell the entire internet the intimate details of your sin.
Wisdom matters.
Privacy matters.
Other people's dignity matters.
But you do need to stop pretending before God.

And for entrenched patterns, bringing the struggle to a trustworthy mature believer, pastor, Christian counselor, or accountability partner may be one of the ways secrecy finally begins losing its oxygen.
James 5:16 speaks about confessing sins to one another and praying for one another.
Sin grows comfortably in darkness.
Healing begins when darkness loses its hiding place.
So perhaps tonight your prayer does not need to be impressive.
Maybe it needs to be brutally simple.
“Jesus, I have been protecting something You died to free me from.”
“Jesus, I don't only want forgiveness for the consequences. Change what I love.”
“Jesus, teach my eyes to belong to You.”
“Jesus, teach my imagination to belong to You.”
“Jesus, teach my body to belong to You.”
“Jesus, expose every excuse I have used to protect this.”
“Jesus, I surrender.”
And if you fail tomorrow?
Get up.
If you fail next week?
Get up.
Not casually.
Not presuming upon grace.
Not saying sin does not matter.
Get up because Christ is still worthy of being pursued.
Proverbs 24:16 says that the righteous falls seven times and rises again.
Your story does not have to end on the floor.
And if you are reading this thinking, “You don't understand what I've watched… what I've imagined… what I've done…”
Maybe I don't.
But the cross does.
The cross is Christianity's declaration that sin is far worse than we wanted to admit and grace is far greater than we dared to hope.
Jesus did not bleed because your sin was insignificant.
He bled because redemption is costly.
First Corinthians 6 speaks with startling clarity about sexual immorality, adultery and other sins, and then Paul says something breathtaking to believers who had come out of sinful lives:
“And such were some of you.”
Were.
Not because their histories had vanished.
Not because their past had never happened.
But because Jesus had interrupted the story.
Paul continues:
“But you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God.”
That is Christianity.
Not:
“Such were some of you, so remain there forever.”
Not:
“Such were some of you, so God could never use you.”
Washed.
Sanctified.
Justified.
Your scandal does not have to receive the final sentence.
Jesus can rewrite what sin tried to finish.
That is why this is bigger than pornography.
Bigger than lust.
Bigger than one hidden tab.
This is about worship.
Who gets your eyes?
Who gets your imagination?
Who gets your body?
Who gets your secret life?
Who gets the version of you nobody else sees?
Jesus does not want merely your Sunday morning.
He wants you.
And what He offers in return is infinitely greater than the temporary satisfaction lust keeps promising and never finally delivers.
If this exposed something hidden, you do not need to describe your private sexual history publicly. But you can draw a line in the sand.
If you need believers to pray for you without knowing every detail, comment, “Pray for me.”

And if Christ has already begun freeing you from a place you once believed would own you forever, tell someone what His grace has done. Your testimony may become the evidence another struggling believer desperately needs that bondage does not have to be permanent.
Not because sharing a Christian article earns favor with God.
It doesn't.
Not because clicking “Share” proves that you are saved.
It doesn't.
Jesus cannot be bought.

But if this truth helped you, sharing it publicly can be one simple way of refusing to be ashamed of Christ and helping biblical truth reach someone whose private battle may be invisible to everybody around them.
There may be a friend on your Facebook list fighting this tonight.
A husband.
A wife.
A teenager.
A church leader.
A lonely believer.
A person who has been silently asking God for help.

Supporting Gospel work can be one practical expression of generosity when it is given freely, worshipfully, and without compulsion. Scripture teaches, “God loves a cheerful giver” in 2 Corinthians 9:7. It does not.
But ministry does require people willing to carry the message with their prayers, voices, generosity, sharing, and faithful participation.
You are helping us point more people toward Him.
Jesus remains the treasure.
Jesus remains the message.
Jesus remains the Savior.
Jesus remains the reason.
If you can support the mission, support it freely and joyfully.
If you cannot, pray.
Share.
Save the truth.
Follow along.
Carry the Gospel wherever God has placed you.
Because somewhere tonight, somebody is sitting in darkness believing the lie that what they have secretly loved has made them too filthy to come home.
Tell them about Jesus.
Tell them about repentance.
Tell them about the cross.
Tell them about the empty tomb.
Tell them that grace does not give us permission to remain chained.
Grace opens the prison door.
And maybe that “somebody” tonight…
is you.
So put down what has been feeding the darkness.
Open your hands.
Stop bargaining.
Stop hiding.
Come into the light.
Jesus already knows the scandal.
And He is still calling sinners to repentance, forgiveness, cleansing, restoration, and a transformed life in Him.
Your lust does not deserve your worship.
Your secret does not deserve your future.
Your shame does not deserve the final word.
Christ does.
And perhaps years from now, when you remember the night you finally stopped defending what was destroying you, you will realize something beautiful:
The secret you thought would become the end of your story became the very place where you discovered how desperately you needed the Savior.
